full_judgment:
2. The preemptor-petitioners sought preemption of the suit land by filing Misc. Case No. 46 of 1981 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the Court of the learned Munsif Barguna which was subsequently renumbered Misc. Case No.5 of 1986 on transfer to the Court of Assistant Judge, Betagi. The preemptor .petitioners filed the aforesaid preemption case mainly on the allegations that they were co-sharer tenants to the disputed holding by inheritance and also by purchase. But late Ismail Khan, another  co-sharer tenant to the disputed holding, transferred  the suit land to his adopted son belonging to a different family, namely, the pre emptee opposite  party No.2, Abdul Jabbar @ Abdus Satter by a  registered deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz dated 14-2-1981. Preemptor-petitioners were not aware of this transaction at the relevant time. But he later having learnt about the same obtained the certified copy of the said Heba-bil-Ewaz and filed said pre-emption case on 11-3-1981. It is further alleged that since the said deed of Heba-bill-Ewaz speaks of payment of consideration money to the extent of Taka 400.00 it was in reality not a deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz but a deed of sale. 

 7. Mr. Md Abdus Sobhan, learned Advocate for the preemptor petitioners, strenuously argues that since consideration money case was passed the deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz in question was a Heba-bil-Ewaz for pecuniary consideration and, as such, suit land was preemptible as it was not covered by the exception mentioned under section 96(10)(C) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Advocate alternatively argues that even if the transaction in question is not considered as a Heba-bil-Ewaz for pecuniary consideration (but a Heba-bil-Ewaz without pecuniary consideration) even then the transaction is not covered by the exception under section 96(10)(c) and the suitland is not exempted from preemption inasmuch as the donee in the present case namely, Abdul Jabbar is admittedly an adopted son of the donor late Ismail Khan and he (donee) is not a relation of the donor by consanguity within three degrees. 

 9. Mr Abdul Quaium, learned Advocate for the opposite party No.1, has, taken us through the plaint, written statement as well as the deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz in question including the deed of cancellation and contends that although an amount of Taka 400.00 is mentioned in the deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz but it is mentioned for the purpose of facilitating registration of the deed as is clear from the deed itself. Hence, mentioning of the said amount could not be considered as a consideration in money in the present case. It is urged by the learned Advocate that the donee namely, the opposite party No. 2 Abdul Jabbar, on the other hand, as it appears from the deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz itself, have Tazbi and the Holy Quran to the donor late Ismail Kha and this should be considered as a consideration passed between the parties and since such consideration was not by way of money paid by the donee Abdul Jabbar, the whole transaction should be considered as a Heba-bil-Ewaz without any pecuniary consideration. Learned Advocate further contends referring to a Division Bench Judgment reported in 11 DLR 353 that a transaction by way of Heba-bil-Ewaz only for consideration of Tazbi, a copy of Holy Quran and Jainamaj even in favour of stranger was covered by the exception under section 96(10)(c) and, as such, the suit land was not preemptible. 

 'Heba-bil-ewaz' for non-pecuniary consideration is not exempted from the operation of section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act unless such 'hiba-bil-ewaz' is in favour of the husband or wife of the testator or the donor or of any relation, by consanguinity, within three degrees of the testator or donor." 

 14. Section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act was bodily lifted and incorporated in section 96(10) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which is reproduced below: 

 17. The contention of Mr Quaium that since Hiba-bil-Ewaz in the present case is made without any pecuniary consideration, even though it is made in favour of the opposite party No.2 is a stranger, the same is covered by the exception provided under section 96(10)(c) and the suit land is not liable to be preempted is not acceptable inasmuch as the decision of the said case does not support him rather it supports the decision of the case reported in 19 DLR 184. Because in the aforesaid 11 DLR 353 case it was held by Amin Ahmed CJ that a transfer in favour of a stranger by Hiba-bil-Ewaj for non-pecuniary consideration is not covered by section 26F(I)(c) of Bengal Tenancy Act which is in terms with section 96(10)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Relevant portion of the decision of the case reported in 11 DLR 353 is quoted below for proper appreciation : 

 "We are unable to accept any of the contentions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. Admittedly, the petitioners are strangers and the hiba-bil-ewaz is not in favour of the husband or wife or the donor or in favour of relations who are by consanguinity within three degrees of the donor. Besides, clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 26F deals with transfer by exchange lease or partition, other than transfer by bequest or gift or hiba as mentioned in clause (C). Clause (C) not only mentions the word "gift" but just after the word "gift", within brackets it is stated "including  hiba but excluding hiba-bil-ewaz for any pecuniary consideration." From the latter provision it is 'very clear, that the Legislature was fully conscious of the distinction between  an ordinary transfer by exchange as mentioned  in clause (b) as distinguished from a hiba or hiba-bil-iwaz for consideration, pecuniary or  otherwise, as contemplated by the Muslim Law Clause (c) not only mentions "gift", but also  states that such gifts shall include all hibas except only hiba-bil-iwaz .for pecuniary  consideration, and that, in the case of all hibas other than hiba-bil-iwaz for pecuniary considerations, the hibas must be in favour of certain relations of the donor. In our opinion, advisedly the Legislature has excluded the hiba-bil-iwaz for pecuniary consideration from the exceptions. As its consideration is simply pecuniary, it is a sale, pure and simple, and it is quite different from a hiba-bil-iwaz in favour of near "relations for non-pecuniary consideration like the exchange of the Quran, etc. This latter kind of hiba, though not stated in so many words, there, is no doubt, is included by implication in the exception contained in clause r (c) and not included in clause (b) under the category of "exchange", otherwise, in spite of provisions of clause (b), the Legislature would , not have used in clause (c) the words "including hiba but excluding hiba-bil-iwaz for any pecuniary consideration". These words have their meaning and cannot be ignored. It seems that it, was the intention of the Legislature to exclude this kind of hiba from the scope of section 26F for preemption, for, they wanted such hiba to take effect like family settlements without giving any right to donor's co-tenants to defeat it by claiming preemption, and, therefore, this privilege or exemption from preemption is allowed only when the donee is husband or wife or consanguinous relation within three degrees."
